quests.title: Raid on Lindisfarne
quests.story: Strange ships with striped sails are heading for a quiet island! Find out who the Vikings were and why they sailed to Lindisfarne.
quests.instruction: Read each question about the raid, then tap the right shield.
quests.hint: Think about where the Vikings sailed from, and what a rich monastery had that they wanted.

questions.ask: In which year did Vikings raid the monastery at Lindisfarne?
questions.fact: News of the raid shocked people across Europe, and it is often seen as the start of the Viking Age.

questions.ask: Lindisfarne is a small island off the coast of which English county today?
questions.fact: At low tide you can walk across the sand to the island, which is also called Holy Island.

questions.ask: Who lived and worked at the monastery on Lindisfarne?
questions.fact: The monks prayed, farmed, studied and made beautiful handwritten books.

questions.ask: Which part of northern Europe did the Vikings come from?
questions.fact: Scandinavia is the area that is today Norway, Denmark and Sweden.

questions.ask: Why did Vikings raid monasteries like Lindisfarne?
questions.fact: Monasteries held gold, silver and jewelled objects, and had no soldiers to guard them.

questions.ask: What were the Vikings' fast wooden ships called?
questions.fact: Longships could cross the open sea and also row up shallow rivers.

questions.ask: Later, many Vikings came to Britain to stay. What were they looking for?
questions.fact: Good farmland was hard to find in parts of Scandinavia, so many Vikings settled in Britain.

questions.ask: Which famous decorated book was made by monks at Lindisfarne?
questions.fact: The Lindisfarne Gospels were made over 1,300 years ago and are kept at the British Library.

questions.ask: Which scholar from York wrote letters full of sadness about the raid?
questions.fact: Alcuin was working for the Frankish king Charlemagne when he heard the news.

questions.ask: Which saint is closely linked with Lindisfarne?
questions.fact: After more raids, the monks left the island, carrying St Cuthbert's coffin with them.

questions.ask: Which year-by-year record of English history tells us about the raid?
questions.fact: The Chronicle was started in King Alfred's time and was added to for over 250 years.

questions.ask: Which sea did the Vikings cross to reach Lindisfarne?
questions.fact: With a good wind, a longship could cross the North Sea in just a few days.

quests.title: Longship Builders
quests.story: The shipyard is busy and the sea is calling! Help the Viking shipbuilders finish their longship, then sail off to explore and trade.
quests.instruction: Read each question about Viking ships, then tap the right crate.
quests.hint: Remember the Vikings had no engines or maps like ours. Think about wood, wind, oars and the sky.

questions.ask: Which wood were most Viking longships built from?
questions.fact: Shipbuilders split oak trunks into long planks using axes and wedges.

questions.ask: What do we call a ship whose planks overlap like tiles on a roof?
questions.fact: Overlapping planks held with iron rivets made the hull strong but able to bend in the waves.

questions.ask: What was a longship's big square sail usually made from?
questions.fact: Spinning and weaving one huge woollen sail took a great deal of time and work.

questions.ask: Which fierce carved head sometimes decorated the front of a longship?
questions.fact: Carved dragon or snake heads on the prow made the ships look frightening to enemies.

questions.ask: Why could longships travel far up shallow rivers?
questions.fact: Longships could even be pulled up onto a beach, so no harbour was needed.

questions.ask: When there was no wind, how did the Vikings move their longship?
questions.fact: Oars poked through holes in the side of the ship, which could be closed when sailing.

questions.ask: How did Viking sailors find their way across the open sea?
questions.fact: They also watched birds, whales and the colour of the water to tell when land was near.

questions.ask: Which Viking explorer reached North America around AD 1000?
questions.fact: Remains of Viking buildings have been found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada.

questions.ask: Vikings sailed down rivers to trade in which great city, now Istanbul?
questions.fact: Some Vikings joined the emperor's bodyguard there, known as the Varangian Guard.

questions.ask: Viking traders reached the markets of which faraway Islamic city?
questions.fact: Thousands of Arab silver coins have been found buried in Viking treasure hoards.

questions.ask: Which Viking ship was found in a burial mound in Norway in 1904?
questions.fact: Two women were buried in the Oseberg ship with a cart, sledges and many fine objects.

questions.ask: The Gokstad ship, found in Norway, had holes for about how many oars?
questions.fact: In 1893 a copy of the Gokstad ship sailed all the way across the Atlantic to America.

quests.title: Alfred and the Danelaw
quests.story: The village storyteller has dropped her scroll, and the story of England is all jumbled! Put nearly 300 years of kings and battles back in order.
quests.instruction: Tap the event that happened first, then the next one.
quests.hint: Think about who came first: the Viking raiders, then Alfred, then his family, then the later kings.

events.label: Lindisfarne raid
events.fact: Vikings attacked the island monastery, and the news shocked people across Europe.

events.label: Great Heathen Army
events.fact: A large Viking army landed in East Anglia and went on to conquer much of England.

events.label: Alfred becomes king
events.fact: Alfred became king of Wessex after his older brother, King Æthelred, died.

events.label: Battle of Edington
events.fact: After hiding in the marshes at Athelney, Alfred beat the Viking leader Guthrum at Edington.

events.label: Danelaw agreed
events.fact: Alfred and Guthrum agreed a border; the Viking-ruled lands became known as the Danelaw.

events.label: Athelstan unites
events.fact: Alfred's grandson Athelstan became the first king to rule all of England.

events.label: Battle of Brunanburh
events.fact: Athelstan beat an alliance of Scots, Vikings from Dublin and Britons from Strathclyde.

events.label: Cnut becomes king
events.fact: Cnut, a Danish prince, became king of England and later of Denmark and Norway too.

events.label: Edward the Confessor
events.fact: Edward, a son of Æthelred the Unready, became king and was known for being very religious.

events.label: Battle of Hastings
events.fact: William of Normandy beat King Harold, and Anglo-Saxon rule of England came to an end.

quests.title: Viking or Saxon?
quests.story: The harbour stalls have got their goods muddled up! Sort out what belongs to the Vikings and what belongs to the Anglo-Saxons.
quests.instruction: Viking or Anglo-Saxon? Tap the right basket for each one.
quests.hint: Think about who sailed in from Scandinavia, and who already ruled the English kingdoms.

questions.ask: A longship with a carved dragon prow
questions.fact: Longships carried Viking raiders, traders and settlers across the seas.

questions.ask: The city of Jorvik
questions.fact: Jorvik was the Viking name for York, which became a busy Viking trading town.

questions.ask: Land ruled by Danish law, called the Danelaw
questions.fact: The Danelaw covered much of northern and eastern England.

questions.ask: Sagas telling of heroes and voyages
questions.fact: Many sagas were written down in Iceland, long after the stories were first told aloud.

questions.ask: Rune stones raised across Scandinavia
questions.fact: Many rune stones were put up to remember family members or great journeys.

questions.ask: Leif Erikson, the explorer
questions.fact: Leif Erikson sailed from Greenland and reached North America around AD 1000.

questions.ask: King Alfred the Great
questions.fact: Alfred is the only English king to be called 'the Great'.

questions.ask: Burhs, the walled towns built for defence
questions.fact: Alfred planned burhs so that no one in Wessex lived more than a day's walk from safety.

questions.ask: Bede, the monk who wrote a history of England
questions.fact: Bede lived at Jarrow and finished his history in AD 731.

questions.ask: The royal ship burial at Sutton Hoo
questions.fact: Sutton Hoo in Suffolk held a famous helmet and is thought to be the grave of King Rædwald.

questions.ask: The Lindisfarne Gospels
questions.fact: This beautiful book was made by Anglo-Saxon monks, probably by a monk called Eadfrith.

questions.ask: Offa's Dyke, the long earth bank
questions.fact: King Offa of Mercia had the dyke built along the border with Wales.

quests.title: Jorvik Market

skill.name: Viking daily life and the city of Jorvik
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Welcome to Jorvik, where the market is buzzing with traders from far and wide! Discover how the Vikings lived, worked and told their stories.
quests.instruction: Read each question about Viking life, then tap the right coin.
quests.hint: Picture a busy Viking town: what people traded, how they paid, and what they believed about their gods.

questions.ask: What did the Vikings call the city we know today as York?
questions.fact: The Romans called it Eboracum, and the Anglo-Saxons called it Eoforwic.

questions.ask: In which year did the Viking Great Army capture York?
questions.fact: York became the capital of a Viking kingdom in the north of England.

questions.ask: In which York street did archaeologists dig up Viking houses from 1976 to 1981?
questions.fact: The wet ground stopped wood, leather and cloth from rotting for over 1,000 years.

questions.ask: What do we call silver chopped into pieces and used to pay for things?
questions.fact: Traders weighed hacksilver on small folding scales to work out what it was worth.

questions.ask: Which golden stone, made from ancient tree sap, did Viking traders bring?
questions.fact: Much of the amber came from the shores of the Baltic Sea and was made into beads.

questions.ask: Which Arctic sea animal's tusks gave Viking traders precious ivory?
questions.fact: Walrus ivory was carved into combs, handles and even chess pieces.

questions.ask: In Scandinavia, many Viking families lived in what kind of home?
questions.fact: A fire burned in the middle of the longhouse, and animals sometimes lived at one end.

questions.ask: What was the Viking meeting called where free men made laws?
questions.fact: Iceland's great Thing, the Althing, first met around AD 930 and still meets today.

questions.ask: Which god did the Vikings believe carried a mighty hammer?
questions.fact: Vikings believed thunder was the sound of Thor's hammer, which was called Mjölnir.

questions.ask: What were the letters of the Viking alphabet called?
questions.fact: Runes were made of straight lines, so they were easy to carve into wood or stone.

questions.ask: Where did Vikings believe brave warriors went after they died?
questions.fact: Vikings believed Valhalla was the god Odin's great hall, where warriors feasted.

questions.ask: Who usually ran a Viking farm and home while the men were away trading?
questions.fact: Unusually for that time, Viking women could own property and ask for a divorce.

quests.title: The Last Saxon Kings

skill.name: Edward the Confessor and the events of 1066
skill.subject: history

quests.story: King Edward has died, and three powerful men all want his crown! Find out what happened in the most famous year in English history.
quests.instruction: Read each question about 1066, then tap the right shield.
quests.hint: Think about the order things happened in 1066, and which claimant came from Norway, Normandy or England.

questions.ask: In which year did Edward the Confessor become king of England?
questions.fact: Edward reigned for about 24 years, until he died in January 1066.

questions.ask: Why was King Edward known as 'the Confessor'?
questions.fact: Edward was made a saint in 1161, nearly 100 years after he died.

questions.ask: Which great church in London did Edward have built?
questions.fact: It was consecrated in December 1065, and nearly every monarch since has been crowned there.

questions.ask: Why was there a struggle for the crown when Edward died?
questions.fact: With no son to follow him, three powerful men each said the crown should be theirs.

questions.ask: Which English earl was crowned king the day after Edward died?
questions.fact: Harold was Earl of Wessex and the brother of Edward's wife, Edith.

questions.ask: Which king of Norway also claimed the English throne in 1066?
questions.fact: His nickname, Hardrada, means 'hard ruler' in Old Norse.

questions.ask: Which duke from France said Edward had promised him the crown?
questions.fact: William's great-aunt Emma was Edward's mother, so the two men were related.

questions.ask: Where did Harold defeat Harald Hardrada in September 1066?
questions.fact: Days later, Harold had to march his tired army hundreds of miles south to face William.

questions.ask: On which date was the Battle of Hastings fought?
questions.fact: The battle lasted most of the day, which was unusually long for that time.

questions.ask: Who won the Battle of Hastings and became king?
questions.fact: William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

questions.ask: Which long embroidered cloth tells the story of 1066 in pictures?
questions.fact: It is about 70 metres long and is kept in the town of Bayeux, in Normandy, France.

questions.ask: What appeared in the sky in April 1066 that some people saw as a sign?
questions.fact: It was Halley's Comet, which returns about every 76 years and appears on the tapestry.

quests.title: City in the Jungle
quests.story: Deep in the rainforest, giant stone pyramids peep above the trees! Explore the great cities of the ancient Maya.
quests.instruction: Read each question about the Maya, then tap the right stone tablet.
quests.hint: Think about the hot, green rainforest of Central America, and the stone cities the Maya built there.

questions.ask: Roughly when was the Classic period, when Maya cities were at their greatest?
questions.fact: At the same time, Britain was ruled by the Romans, then the Anglo-Saxons and Vikings.

questions.ask: In which part of the world did the ancient Maya live?
questions.fact: Maya lands covered parts of today's Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras and El Salvador.

questions.ask: Which great Maya city in Guatemala has temples rising above the rainforest?
questions.fact: Tikal's tallest temple is about 65 metres high, taller than Nelson's Column.

questions.ask: What shape were the big Maya temples?
questions.fact: A small temple sat on top, where kings and priests held ceremonies.

questions.ask: Which king of Palenque was buried in a tomb deep inside a pyramid?
questions.fact: K'inich Janaab' Pakal became king aged 12 and ruled from AD 615 to 683.

questions.ask: What was the most important crop grown by Maya farmers?
questions.fact: Maya stories told that the first people were made from maize dough.

questions.ask: In the Maya ball game, which part of the body did players mostly hit the ball with?
questions.fact: The heavy ball was made of rubber from rainforest trees.

questions.ask: Each Maya city had its own ruler. What do historians call this kind of city?
questions.fact: Powerful city-states such as Tikal and Calakmul were often rivals.

questions.ask: Which Maya city in Mexico has the famous pyramid El Castillo?
questions.fact: At the spring and autumn equinoxes, a shadow like a snake seems to slide down its steps.

questions.ask: What kind of land surrounded many Maya cities?
questions.fact: Jaguars, monkeys and brightly coloured quetzal birds lived in the forests.

questions.ask: What happened to many Maya cities in the south around AD 900?
questions.fact: Historians think droughts, wars and too many people may all have played a part.

questions.ask: What is true of the Maya people today?
questions.fact: Millions of Maya people still live in Central America and speak Maya languages.

quests.title: Maya Number Keepers
quests.story: The royal scribes need a helper! Learn to count with dots, bars and shells, and read the secrets of the Maya calendars.
quests.instruction: Read each question about Maya numbers, then tap the right pot.
quests.hint: Remember: a dot is small, a bar is bigger, and a shell means nothing at all. Count up carefully.

questions.ask: In Maya numbers, what did a single dot stand for?
questions.fact: Three dots side by side meant the number 3.

questions.ask: In Maya numbers, what did a bar stand for?
questions.fact: A bar with two dots above it showed the number 7.

questions.ask: How would a Maya scribe write the number 10?
questions.fact: Numbers up to 19 used bars and dots; bigger numbers were stacked in levels.

questions.ask: Which symbol did the Maya use for zero?
questions.fact: The Maya were one of the first peoples in the world to use a symbol for zero.

questions.ask: Maya counting was based on groups of which number?
questions.fact: Counting on both fingers and toes makes twenty, which may be how it began.

questions.ask: How many days were in the Maya solar calendar, the Haab'?
questions.fact: The Haab' had 18 months of 20 days, plus 5 extra days at the end.

questions.ask: How many days were in the sacred Maya calendar, the Tzolk'in?
questions.fact: Both calendars fitted together in a great cycle that lasted 52 years.

questions.ask: What do we call the picture-signs the Maya used for writing?
questions.fact: Maya glyphs could stand for whole words or for the sounds of syllables.

questions.ask: What were Maya folding books, called codices, made from?
questions.fact: Only four Maya codices survive today; most were destroyed in the 1500s.

questions.ask: Which beans did the Maya grind to make a frothy drink?
questions.fact: The Maya poured the drink from pot to pot to make froth on top.

questions.ask: Besides making drinks, how were cacao beans sometimes used?
questions.fact: Cacao beans are what we still use to make chocolate today.

questions.ask: Which planet did Maya astronomers track very carefully?
questions.fact: A Maya book called the Dresden Codex has tables showing when Venus would appear.

quests.title: Maya or Anglo-Saxon?

skill.name: Comparing the Maya with Anglo-Saxon Britain
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Two worlds, one moment in time! Around AD 900, life in the Maya rainforest and in Anglo-Saxon England was very different. Can you tell them apart?
quests.instruction: Maya or Anglo-Saxon? Tap the right basket for each one.
quests.hint: Ask yourself: is this from a hot rainforest in Central America, or a cool, green English village?

questions.ask: Stone pyramid cities home to tens of thousands
questions.fact: Big Maya cities had plazas, palaces and pyramids built from limestone.

questions.ask: Fields of maize
questions.fact: Maize was ground into dough to make tortillas and tamales.

questions.ask: Jaguars prowling the rainforest
questions.fact: Maya kings sometimes wore jaguar skins to show their power.

questions.ask: A shell symbol meaning zero
questions.fact: Zero let Maya astronomers write down very large numbers.

questions.ask: A frothy chocolate drink
questions.fact: Maya chocolate was bitter, not sweet, and was sometimes flavoured with chilli.

questions.ask: Ball courts for a sacred game
questions.fact: Ball courts had long sloping walls, and some had stone rings high up.

questions.ask: Small villages of wooden, thatched houses
questions.fact: Most Anglo-Saxon villages had only a few families living in them.

questions.ask: Fields of wheat and barley
questions.fact: Wheat was baked into bread, and barley was used for brewing ale.

questions.ask: Wolves roaming the woodland
questions.fact: Wolves still lived wild in England in Anglo-Saxon times.

questions.ask: Roman numerals, with no zero
questions.fact: Monks wrote numbers using Roman letters such as I, V, X and C.

questions.ask: Mead made from honey
questions.fact: Mead was drunk at feasts in a lord's great hall.

questions.ask: Monks copying books in Latin
questions.fact: Monks wrote with quill pens on parchment made from animal skin.

quests.title: Victorian Inventors
quests.story: Steam whistles, ticking clocks and gas lamps fill the street! Meet the inventors, builders and writers who changed Britain in Queen Victoria's time.
quests.instruction: Read each question about the Victorians, then tap the right coin.
quests.hint: Think about steam, railways and factories, and how life slowly got better for Victorian children.

questions.ask: When did Queen Victoria reign?
questions.fact: Victoria reigned for 63 years, longer than any British monarch before her.

questions.ask: Which father and son built the famous steam engine Rocket in 1829?
questions.fact: Rocket won the Rainhill Trials, reaching about 30 miles per hour.

questions.ask: Which engineer built the Great Western Railway?
questions.fact: Brunel also designed the SS Great Britain, one of the first big iron ships with a propeller.

questions.ask: Which fuel was burned to power most Victorian steam engines?
questions.fact: Burning coal boiled water, and the steam pushed pistons to make engines move.

questions.ask: In which giant glass building was the Great Exhibition of 1851 held?
questions.fact: The Crystal Palace was built of iron and glass in Hyde Park, London.

questions.ask: Which member of the royal family helped organise the Great Exhibition?
questions.fact: Over six million visits were made to the exhibition in under six months.

questions.ask: What was the Penny Black, first used in 1840?
questions.fact: It was the world's first sticky postage stamp, showing the young Queen Victoria.

questions.ask: Who invented the telephone in 1876?
questions.fact: Bell was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, and later moved to Canada and the USA.

questions.ask: Why did many factory and mine owners hire young children?
questions.fact: Small children could crawl under machines and through narrow tunnels in mines.

questions.ask: What were the laws passed to protect children in factories called?
questions.fact: The Factory Act of 1833 banned children under 9 from working in textile mills.

questions.ask: From 1880, what did all children aged 5 to 10 have to do?
questions.fact: Victorian pupils often wrote on slates with chalk and copied from the blackboard.

questions.ask: Which Victorian author wrote Oliver Twist?
questions.fact: Dickens worked in a boot-polish factory when he was just 12 years old.
